Lecture 4: Lagrange multipliers

These are the notes for the fourth lecture of the course. They cover the method of Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimisation and are intended to be read alongside chapter 7 of the set text.

Suppose we wish to find the maximum of f(x, y) subject to the constraint g(x, y) = c. At a constrained maximum the level curve of f through the point must be tangent to the constraint curve, for otherwise we could move along the constraint and increase f.

Tangency of the two curves means their normals are parallel, so the gradients satisfy grad f = lambda grad g for some scalar lambda, the Lagrange multiplier. Together with the constraint itself this gives three equations in the three unknowns x, y and lambda.

Worked examples

Example 1. Maximise f(x, y) = xy subject to x + y = 10. The gradient condition gives y = lambda and x = lambda, so x = y, and the constraint gives x = y = 5. The maximum value is 25.

Example 2. Find the point on the plane x + 2y + 2z = 9 nearest the origin. Minimise the squared distance x^2 + y^2 + z^2; the gradient condition gives (2x, 2y, 2z) = lambda (1, 2, 2), so the point is (1, 2, 2) and its distance from the origin is 3.

Remarks

The multiplier has a useful interpretation: lambda is the rate at which the optimal value of f changes as the constraint level c is relaxed. In economics it is the shadow price of the constrained resource.

With several constraints g1 = c1, ..., gk = ck the condition becomes grad f = lambda1 grad g1 + ... + lambdak grad gk, provided the constraint gradients are linearly independent at the point. When they are not, the method can miss the optimum, as the exercises show.

Second-order conditions, which distinguish maxima from minima and saddle points, use the bordered Hessian. We will not need them this term; for the problems on the sheet it is enough to compare the values of f at each critical point and, where the constraint set is unbounded, to check the behaviour at infinity.

Exercises for the supervision: questions 3, 4, 7 and 9 from sheet 4. Question 9 is harder than it looks; think about what happens where the gradient of the constraint vanishes.
